newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic's vital propaganda machine under threat.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic's vital propaganda machine under threat.

text.p: The Serbian state propaganda machine seen as vital for President Slobodan Milosevic's continued hold on power has become a primary target in the wave of political unrest sweeping the country.

The president's authoritarian Socialist Party (SPS) annulled opposition election victories in 14 major towns, provoking mass protests, in part because it fears losing control of influential regional media outlets, diplomats say.

Even in towns where municipal election wins by the opposition were allowed to stand, disputes have erupted over SPS machinations to frustrate takeovers of local radio and television by political rivals.

Local security police in the city of Kragujevac loyal only to Milosevic flooded the regional radio and television station (RTK) this week to prevent editors named by the new local authorities from taking charge.

Protesters blocked the main highway into Kragujevac, south of Belgrade, but were clubbed aside by riot police sent from the capital, while Serbian state television appealed to a pliant state court to stall any handover of RTK.

Serbia's democracy movement, led by the Zajedno (Together) coalition, has had a hard time spreading its message beyond a few large cities because of Milosevic's stranglehold on the mainstream media, especially Serbian state television (RTS).
RTS, virtually the only source of news for the less educated, small-town and rural majority of Serbia's population, has ignored, minimised or vilified opposition demonstrations.
It has accused peaceful protesters of being "terrorists" in the pay of Western circles bent on destabilising federal Yugoslavia, which groups Serbia and small Montenegro.

The power of RTS to mislead or smother unwanted news was highlighted when provincial SPS supporters bused into Belgrade to counter Zajedno rallies told reporters they had no idea people had been protesting for weeks or what the issues were.

Even Belgraders might have been denied information about the chanting crowds surging down their streets every day if a Socialist attempt to silence the capital's two main independent radio stations had succeeded.

Radios B-92 and Index, whose transmitters are too weak to reach beyond metropolitan Belgrade, were knocked off the air in early December because of what the state news agency Tanjug called "heavy rains in the past few days".

But Socialist authorities turned the stations' transmitters back on to calm a storm of international criticism and after realising that B-92 had partly outwitted the ban by sending out reports on the Internet.

While state radio and television have been uniformly contemptuous of protests, hints of dissension have emerged in one hitherto slavishly pro-government newspaper, the main afternoon daily Vecernje Novosti.

Since early January, Vecernje Novosti has provided expanded coverage of the protest campaign with strikingly neutral reporting in what some analysts say betrays splits in an increasingly discredited ruling class.
Milosevic's grip on the media was crucial in maintaining SPS power during the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in which Croatia and Bosnia seceded from the Serbian-led federation.
Rulers in Croatia and Bosnia applied similar controls on local media to whip up their own nationalist fervour.

Milosevic's main tactics in frustrating a widespread growth of independent media have been withholding broadcast licences, curbing printing and distribution facilities and engineering state takeovers through the courts.
The few independent newspapers and magazines are much more expensive than state-run counterparts because of their tiny circulations and excessive distribution costs.
That means they are read mainly by Serbia's small urban intelligentsia, who have little political clout.
